entries.title: Port routes between a planet and its moons
entries.body:
Only the legacy planner flew between a planet and its moons; it was deleted in T175. Read
it at `412f938` (`lib/Iapetus/Solver/Crossing.hs`, `Plan.hs` `route`/`methodsFor`,
`Steer.hs`) with [Half-Turn Transfers](../wiki/reference/Half-Turn%20Transfers.md).
Port: the crossing into a child and the climb out of a moon into an orbit around its
parent (`climbTo`); the half-turn doctrine (`heldPlane`, the injection fan at three
quarters of the Hohmann time, `crossingFraction`), with `Lambert.planInPlane`, kept in
the kernel for it; the staging ellipse (`stagingRadii`); and the moon floors' aim
allowance, `2·sphere/flight` (`Oberth.aimAllowance`, deleted). Acceptance, from the
legacy `test/Main.hs` at `412f938` (crossings L2474–2562, plan laws L2748–2995): LEO to
Luna, injection under 4.5 km/s and the cheapest 3.5–5.5 km/s; Titan by way of Saturn,
staged in an ellipse, under 14.5 km/s, handing off at Earth, Saturn and Titan; the climb
from Luna to ten Earth radii 1.4–1.6 km/s (the dearest under 1.8); Luna to Mars by way
of Earth 6.5–8.0 km/s; every route real and valid.

entries.title: Port multi-pass, powered and real-date flybys
entries.body:
The planner's assist (`Strategies.viaAssist`) passes one body once; the legacy flyby solver
(`Solver/Flyby.hs`, `Maneuver/PoweredFlyby.hs` at `412f938`, deleted in T175) also
priced a powered pass and chained passes on real dates. Port them, reading
[Voyager 2 Reference](../wiki/reference/Voyager%202%20Reference.md). Acceptance, from the
legacy `test/Main.hs` at `412f938` (L2380–2461): Voyager 2's Jupiter pass settles at both
spheres with a periapsis of 640,000–750,000 km and a periapsis impulse under 100 m/s,
handing off at Earth and Jupiter; the grand tour's four legs (launch −8168.9 d, Jupiter
−7480.56, Saturn −6702.36, Uranus −5089.75, Neptune −3781.34 d from J2000) fly as one
real, valid path, handing off at Earth, Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus, with 20–40 t of
propellant left.

entries.title: Port single-body orbit changes
entries.body:
The planner reaches another body; only the legacy solvers changed an orbit around one
body (`Solver.hohmannTo`, `biEllipticTo`, `alignTo`; `Maneuver/Shift.hs` and
`Station.hs` at `412f938`, deleted in T175). Port them as strategies for an objective at
the body the ship is at. Acceptance, from the legacy `test/Main.hs` at `412f938`: the
solver laws (L2093–2277), each shift arriving on its target circle or plane and pricing
as its plan, and a chemical stage flying each as a real, valid path; Hohmann cheaper
than bi-elliptic from 7,000 to 14,000 km with a 100,000 km apex; the station descent at
Mars from its sphere to 20,428 km at 599.7 m/s over 2.48e6 s; the plane alignment
burning at the planes' intersection within one period.

entries.title: Strategy study: every HTN strategy in the literature, per compound task, ship class and band
entries.body:
Shaun asked for a full, literature-backed list of the strategies the outer layer should have,
for every compound task (departure, capture, crossings, flybys, rendezvous, in-well changes,
surface, staging, waiting, aborts, tours, external momentum) against every band and ship class,
then to implement them slowly. The 22-strategy catalogue in `Flight Regimes.md` was written from
mission practice and is checked against, not taken as the answer. Research only, no code, in
`docs/strategy-study/` (brief in its README): seven reports, then `summary.md` with the matrix
and the implementation order, then wiki rows and tasks. T216–T219 (capture) stand; the study may
reorder them.

*2026-10-01:* the seven reports and `summary.md` are written (about 120 strategies, prerequisites
P1–P19, 14 waves, 11 open questions). Next, after Shaun reads it: the wiki rows, the corrections
he approves, and a task per wave.

entries.title: Retire the legacy planner and rename Outer
entries.body:
T123's first half, in four commits after the audit variants (T155–T157).
- **Moved.** The craft presets and modifiers to `Iapetus.Craft.Presets`; `Play.summary`
  into `Iapetus.Trace.Document` (the document's `summary`); `Solver.Windows` to
  `Iapetus.Windows` with its own `ScanError` (`Unavailable`, `Playback`, `Quantity`),
  which `Example`'s `Scanning` takes; the patched-conic convention's reason, known only
  to the flyby solver, beside `Reach.sphereJoin`. `Search.Pareto` keeps `Measures`,
  `costOf` and `kneeOf`; its pruning went with `Plan`.
- **Deleted.** `Plan`, `Steer`, `Solver`, `Solver.Crossing`, `Solver.Flyby`,
  `Search.Stepper`, `Maneuver.Shift`, `Maneuver.Station`, `Maneuver.PoweredFlyby`,
  `Play`; the kernel exports left without a caller: `Burn.integrateGuided`,
  `Burn.matchAsymptote`, `Kepler.conicPlaneNormal`, `Oberth.aimAllowance`,
  `Path.frameAt`, `Path.arcConic`; `Realise.burnArc` is private now. With
  `integrateGuided` went its measured 0.27% waste (about 13.5 m/s on a 5 km/s burn,
  velocity to go flipping sign at the last short steps' fourth stage); the thrust law
  (LR014) now covers three integrators, programme, along and tangential, and LR014's
  wording, which names none, still reads true.
- **Kept, against the plan's list.** `Path.splice`/`SpliceError`: the kernel's path and
  realise laws build their kicked paths with it. `Lambert.planInPlane`: kernel, tested,
  and the held plane the moon routes' port (T176) needs.
- **Renamed.** `Iapetus.Outer.X` is `Iapetus.X`; `test/Outer.hs` is `test/Planner.hs`,
  `test/Main.hs`'s kept groups `test/Kernel.hs`, and `test/Main.hs` wires the catalogue,
  kernel and planner suites. Kernel's trace-document tests fly the planner's worked
  example, the one planner fixture in Kernel. LR001, LR011 (its grep now lists the
  planner's modules), the five `enforced-by` entries, AGENTS.md, the skill's triggers,
  README (its GHCi session is now the worked example), the cabal description and seven
  wiki pages follow the rename.
- **Tests.** 229 → 184: the stepper, solver laws, flybys, grand tour, crossings,
  steering, plan laws, asymptote guidance, and the Shift and Station cases went; their
  acceptance figures are in the port tasks T176–T178, with the legacy code at `412f938`.
  Forced `-j4` rebuild warning-clean after each step; trace JSON and text byte-identical
  to the audit variants' commit over fifteen scenarios (three exported menus); the
  viewer's 32 Playwright specs pass.
- **Left broken, as the user accepted.** The denotational-design guide still names the
  legacy modules (`Iapetus.Play`, `Solver`, `Plan`, `Search.Stepper`: chapter 9's module
  map, chapter 10's toolbox, chapters 8 and 12, appendix B); its companion package does
  not depend on `iapetus`.

entries.title: Viewer mockups and ship concepts
entries.body:
- **Viewer mockups** in `docs/archive/viewer-mockups/` (index at `index.html`,
  published under `/www/doc/iapetus/viewer-mockups/`): four working pages
  over the committed Earth-to-Mars trace that drive the viewer's own
  `Trace` and `Scene` — A quiet map, B flight log, C telemetry HUD,
  D compare flights (D's other routes illustrative). A shared data layer
  (`shared.js`) derives per-arc, per-burn and per-leg numbers, the ship's
  reading at an instant, a mass-continuity check, and the thrust
  direction during burns from the integrator steps (dv/dt − g(r); 12.03
  against F/m = 12.00 m/s² mid escape burn), drawn as a heading chevron
  with a plume. What they found: the capture burn's mass jump (Q152), coasts
  drawn kinked by time-uniform sampling (up to 11.5° per vertex, 122 km
  off; anomaly sampling 0.5°, 3 km), planets vanishing zoomed out, label
  pile-up, local mode's drift (Q86→A105), spirals labelled "RIDE". Next:
  [viewer-views.md](../docs/plans/viewer-views.md) (A101).
- **Ship concepts** in `docs/archive/ship-concepts/` (uncommitted; published under
  `/www/doc/iapetus/ship-concepts/` with a 3D viewer): four example craft
  built by Blender scripts over a small kit (`kit/shipkit.py`), exported as
  GLB, FBX, OBJ and .blend with named parts and `socket_*` attach points —
  Longsight NEP surveyor (Long Survey), Kestrel NTR tug sized to the
  sample trace's craft and laid out for FDM printing (Industrial
  Footholds), Mule salt-water hauler (Solar Network), Lantern D–³He torch
  corvette (Threshold). Each has a design note tying its layout to the
  wiki's cards and heat rules; `renders/lineup.png` shows them at true
  scale.

entries.title: The gate's estimate holds at the member as it does at the seed
entries.body:
**Question** **Q47. Does the sweep-loss estimate hold against the realiser?**
*(2026-09-26)* The gate now prices a pass's waste as  − sin(θ/2)/(θ/2)@
of its Δv, the fixed-aim estimate, and the menu quotes it. Step 3 flies
these passes through the realiser; compare the Δv the tank pays with the
impulse and the estimate, over sweeps from 20° to 70°, before the
estimate decides anything more than the order of a menu. Owner: the
outer layer proof of concept, step 3.
*First data 2026-09-26 (step 3a, the realiser's correction against the
estimate):* 11° sweep 5.7 against 5.8 m/s; 21° to 28° on the torch a
constant 3.9 against 4.0 to 7.3; 30° 6.5 against 11.4; 38° 8.3 against
19.4; 46° 38 against 42; 51° 45 against 65. The estimate bounded the
correction every time, by one to two and a half. The correction mixes the
energy shortfall with the drift's velocity signature; measure the
achieved excess against the planned one next.
*Energy data 2026-09-26 (step 3b, the burn's energy miss at cutoff as
Δv):* from a circular orbit the estimate is exact, 18° 15.0 against
15.1 m/s and 46° 42.4 against 42.2; on the eccentric ellipses of later
passes it overshoots, 51° 50 against 65 and the torch's equal passes a
constant 4 against 4 to 7. The cause is the rate: the estimate sweeps at
the perigee's angular rate, and on an ellipse the burn's mean rate is
lower. Candidate fix: read the sweep as the true anomaly the burn spans
on its own conic, not ω at the impulse times the burn's clock.
*Read off the conic 2026-09-27 (A053):* the sweep is now the velocity's
turn over the coasting conic, so the estimate no longer sweeps at the
perigee's rate; the torch's 5638 m/s capture read 405° and now 14°. New
data: a 12.4° turn burn on the torch, 50° sweep, correction 44.6 against
an estimate of 51.7 m/s. Open still: on a braking burn the coasting
estimate understates the flown sweep (14° estimated, 43° flown, since the
burn slows the ship), and the estimate is still to be compared with what
the full solve pays over a range of sweeps.
*Measured at the seed 2026-09-27 (A054):* the gate integrates the burn
and reads the energy shortfall as Δv, so the menu's waste is a measurement
of the seed's burn, not an estimate. What remains open is the seed against
the member: the solve moves the burn, and the waste it finally pays is the
join's to read (A050). The sweep-loss formula stays as the flight report's
yardstick beside the correction, and as the reading where a burn is not
flown.
*Closed form again 2026-09-27 (A056):* the gate estimates the waste on
the half-impulse conic and a test holds it within the margin of the
integrated burn over circles, ellipses and hyperbolas; the widest gap is
the torch's 77° escape, read at 348 against 484 m/s measured.
*Closed 2026-09-27 (A074):* measured over 196 finite burns on 55
converged routes of four fixtures, at the seed and at the member. Where
the reading's conic turns as far as the flight does, every held burn
reads within the margin of its flown waste at both points (×0.80–0.96
on escapes and passes, ×1.06–1.47 on brakes, the member moving the ratio
by under 0.02) and every rotating burn's saving against the held aim is
within the margin (×0.68–1.00); beyond it lie the torch's 9157 m/s
escape after a 47.7° turn (66° read, 153° flown, 11.9 percent read
against 31.4 flown) and the helium torch's 4802 m/s brachistochrone
escape (47° read, 112° flown, 8.3 against 19.2), and the parent-field
burns, whose sign the two do not agree on. The flown excess leaves
0.2–2.1° off the sized direction on a held aim and 2.4–5.4° on a
rotating one, 1.2 to 7.6 percent of the burn if bought at the sphere,
and 13.4° (23.5 percent) on the torch's extreme; nothing is bought,
since the join reads the asymptote reached and the member's burn grows
by its energy waste alone (the torch's three passes: 57 against 59
m/s). Q141 holds the residue.
*Literature and the rotating aim 2026-09-27 (A073):* the estimate's
structure is Robbins's; the 2019 thesis found his bound about a quarter
over the steered losses and under the held aim's at long burns, which
is the sign of our 77° gap. With the aim rotating (`readTurning`) the
reading is held to its oracle by the ordering against the held aim and
the saving between them, both within the margin over the same thirty
cases; its own miss on long brakes is the fall inward a fixed conic
cannot see (Q141).

**Answer** **The gate's estimate holds at the member as it does at the seed; the flown excess leaves up to five degrees off the direction its impulse was sized for, and nothing is bought for that downstream.** *(
step 5, twenty-first part; closes Q47)* Q47 asked two things the gate's
closed form (A056) had not been measured on: whether the burn the full
solve settles on wastes what the estimate said at the seed, and whether
the flown burn leaves with the planned excess direction and what a miss
there costs downstream. The measurement is the `q47` group in
`test/Outer.hs`: four fixtures (the D–T torch from low orbit, the
nuclear-thermal stack scaled by five, the nuclear-thermal, and the
helium-3 torch parked at 36,000 km bound for a 20,000 km band), every
route of each menu whose skeleton builds, whose cheap solve prices whole
and whose full solve converges (55 routes: 29, 15, 4 and 7), and every
event on them flown under a held or a rotating aim, 196 burns in all,
each read at the seed and at the member. The estimate is `readBurn` or
`readTurning` with the fixture's craft scaled to the mass the flight's
first step carries (at the seed that is the cheap solve's
`BurnRead.mass`, printed beside it and equal on every row), the event's
state and its impulse; the flown waste is `measureBurn`'s computation on
the skeleton's own flight, the energy the burn fell short of its impulse
by, signed by the change the impulse meant, as Δv at cutoff; both as
shares of the burn's Δv. The criterion is the oracle test's (A056):
within the margin where the flown share exceeds a fifth of the
tol
…[truncated]

entries.title: A leg kind means a set of flight paths; forms represent it, and the planner picks forms up front by what the start guarantees

meta.revisit-if: two forms of one kind cannot be made to agree on their overlap, or a structural guarantee is needed that no type can carry

entries.body:
**Question** _(None asked: settled in step 3's design talk with Shaun, and checked against the denotational-design
guide, chapters 8, 9 and 13.)_ How does the library hold several ways to build one leg, and who decides which is used?

**Answer**
- **The planner (the HTN) builds the problem's shape.** The ship's start is the world's state, fixed however awkward it
  is. Every later state is a choice. Where the planner has that freedom, it offers alternatives built from forms that
  are fast or stable for the case. The solver only solves the problem it is handed and never decides the structure.
- **A leg kind is a meaning:** for a start, the set of easy-reading flight paths that do the job. For the impulsive
  escape, a path is a coast on the start's orbit, one burn at the departure hyperbola's periapsis, then out to the
  sphere. Events are questions asked of a path (where was the burn, where was the exit). Every form returns the kind's
  event record, and its events are exactly those of the path it stands for (R004).
- **A form is one representation of a kind:** its own variables, rows, seeds and choices. It makes two promises at
  every start it accepts:
  - **soundness:** nothing wrong, so every path it gives is of the kind;
  - **completeness:** nothing missing, so over all its choices it gives every path of the kind. Otherwise a cheaper
    route is silently never offered.

  Two honest forms therefore agree wherever both apply, which is the cheap test (as chapter 9's forms and chapter 8's
  corrector against Hohmann). A physically different leg (a burn away from periapsis, a dogleg) is a different kind.
- **Choices are physical questions about a path,** defined once for the kind, so every form answers to the same
  definition. The escape's sense is the sign of ĥ·n̂. Its lap is "the opportunity nearest t_aim", never relative to a
  seed. Situation limits such as "not before t_ready" are keeps, not choices.
- **Two kinds of domain:**
  - **A value domain** says it works for these numbers. It is checked at each evaluation, and gives a typed reason
    outside (chapter 13, clause 4). For example, an asymptote beyond the cone's reach.
  - **A structural domain** says it works for this kind of start, for every value the solver could try. No check on
    numbers can promise that, so it is a type (`CircleStart`). Only the world or a form built to guarantee it can make
    one.
- **Guarantees are by construction only.** A capture that parks on a circle produces a `CircleStart` only if it has one
  radius variable. Two radii with an equality row are circular only once converged. Two radii held equal can be
  released by revision. A form that claims a guarantee is tested for it: every end it produces, at any values, has the
  promised shape.
- **Easier to solve is not cheaper.** The circle pairing (a capture onto a circle, then the circle escape) is offered
  beside the general one (an ellipse, then the escape from any conic), and the menu compares them (R002, R003).
  A standing preference for circles, "players like circles, and ships carry Δv for it", is an input from the game or
  the player through the objective or the default parked orbit (Q187), never the planner's own arithmetic.

**Why:** a single general interface throws away forms that are cheap and stable where they apply. Stating the meaning
first makes "the same leg" testable, and stating choices and guarantees on the meaning lets the planner chain forms
safely.

**Alternatives considered:** one general form per leg (simpler, but slower and less stable in the common cases); the
solver choosing the structure (it can't know the whole plan, and its arithmetic would choose silently, R002); a
structural domain as a run-time check (it can't promise "for every value"); a choice relative to the seed (the
meaning would then depend on where the solve started).

entries.title: Scoped names and handles between legs
entries.body:
A166. First the design with the denotational-design skill: the meaning of a local name, a
handle and a slot. Then the pass over every leg: joins take handles from the legs they
join (the excess, the entry state, the mass T103 threads) instead of reading global
strings; `Refine` scopes each leg's events, variables and pins by its path in the plan
tree at assembly; the assist's hand-written suffixes go. Before the first route that holds
a sub-part twice (a two-hop journey, two assists, a refuelling stop). After T103, which
already passes over every leg.

*2026-09-30 (A171):* the direct leg read the exit's instant from "t2", which a spiral escape
does not own; it now reads the escape's `leaving` closure. `Situation.exitDelivered` is a
second piece the escape hands on (whether the excess was chosen); fold both into the
handle. The escape legs still read "t2" among themselves, as do other legs' joins.

entries.title: Step 0: the skeleton's meaning, with no physics
entries.body:
Variables, holds, conditions and the membership check, tested on a toy. Design note:
`docs/plans/rebuild/step-0-skeleton.md`, reviewed by Shaun 2026-10-04 (handles from A166, the five open points as
recommended).

`Iapetus.Planner.Problem` (450 lines) and `test/Rebuild.hs`: the six laws of the note plus the leg-from-scope
and malformed-problem tests, and the boundary tests (R009, R012, and only `Units` importing units). 15 pass; the
whole suite, 223. Clean under hlint. Differences from the note, recorded there: rows need `Ord` for domain checks, a condition's reason
for having no value and a hold's reason are the problem's type parameters (`Problem why held`) rather than text, holds and seeds are partial maps
by slot apart from the variables, `start` names any free variable left unseeded, conditions declare their row
count, and `problem` refuses malformed problems.

entries.title: The phasing loop's impulses as events on the ledger
entries.body:
Found by T103. The phasing loop's two small impulses are the lowering's, not events, so
the ledger does not spend them and the escape after a loop starts heavier than the loop
left the ship; the mass-chain test leaves routes with a loop out. Make them events (or
charge them on the ledger) so the chain holds there too.

Viewer mass readouts
entries.body: They wait on burns starting at the mass the earlier burns flew.

entries.title: The spiral capture's fall and spiral keep the seed's mass, not the mass the brake before them achieved
entries.body:
A spiral capture's fall and spiral fly at the mass the burns before them achieved, read from the ledger (LR009). It was
shaped once at the strategy's estimate; the solve then moved the burns before it:
- the low-ceiling torch's fall started 10 kg lighter than its brake left it (389–1,659 kg before T224);
- the electric freighter's started 233.8 kg heavier than its cruise left it.

**Held ceiling (merge 38183c6).** Where the throttle holds the ceiling throughout at both masses, the path does not depend
on the mass (LR014), so the mass samples scale by achieved over estimate, exactly.

**Full thrust (merge 05e5772).** The fall is re-settled at the ledger's mass. `Fall.resettle` runs the build's rounds of
the fixed point from no propellant under its last step guard, both frozen, so it is smooth in the mass (LR006). Readers:
- the cruise's entry (`entryAt`, now on values) re-settles once per reading;
- the capture's fall flight re-settles once per reading;
- the spiral's start, mass and spans and the entry join read the fall's memoised flight;
- what the leg is (fall, averaged spiral) stays the build's, since a radius read back off a flight sits on the circle
  only to rounding.

Measured on the electric mission:
- solve 3.8 s (main 0.79 s; 5.8 s re-settled in every form);
- mass gap 3×10⁻⁸ kg;
- final mass 21,749.6 kg (main overstated it at 21,969.6).

Option 2 (rebuild and re-solve) was also exact: solves 0.93 s, but each rebuild re-ran the whole refinement (1.15 s).
The two options differed by 0.3 kg and 8.4 h only because the member is not unique (slack 89; the minimum-norm step lands
nearest its start). Experiments kept as tags `archive/t225-diag`, `archive/t225-opt1` and `archive/t225-opt2`.

Findings:
- The settle takes 5 rounds; a warm start would save about one.
- One re-settle per reading would couple the cruise's entry to the capture's event, a loop through the fall's rotation.
- The low-ceiling torch and the electric mission both assert the mass chain to a milligram now.

entries.title: A burn's centroid lead cancels catastrophically for short low-flow burns
entries.body:
Found when the spiral line moved (A173) and the electric mission's cruise solved onto a
member with three segments at their one-second floor (2.4, 2.8 and 3.6 s): the lowered path
put o.25's burn before o.24's (`EpochsDisjoint`). `Burn.centroidLead` computed
m₀/ṁ − T/ln(m₀/m₁) plainly; for the electric freighter m₀/ṁ ≈ 4.5·10⁸ s and a two-second
burn's mass ratio is 1 + 5·10⁻⁹, so the logarithm kept eight digits and the centroid came
out ten seconds late (62 s for a 0.01 s burn). The throttled branch's
m₀·ln(m₀/m_c) − (m₀ − m_c) cancelled the same way for a short full-thrust phase. Now both
read x = ṁt/m₀ through `log1p`, with their series below x = 0.01. Test: "a burn's centroid
lies within it however short the burn and however slow the flow" (fails on the old form).
It also cleared a false "breaks leg order" reading on one helium-torch route.

entries.title: Investigate a memo of porkchop cells on an absolute lattice, shared across crafts and later searches
entries.body:
Shaun, 2026-10-02: a porkchop scan sweeps mostly over time, so another search a week later (or by another ship) overlaps
the last one. Would a memo of cells hit?
- **Not today.** `Windows.scanBetween` lays departures from the order's own epoch (`opens`), over a synodic period in
  steps of synodic/cells, and the flight range from the bodies' elements at `opens`. A later search shifts both off the
  old cells, so exact inputs almost never repeat.
- **What to investigate:**
  - departures on a fixed lattice (multiples of a step from J2000), and each body pair's flight range and step from its
    mean elements, not the search's start: about 99% of a 780-day Mars synodic period's columns would repeat a week later;
  - a cache of Lambert cells keyed by (bodies, departure epoch, flight time). These are craft-independent, so one cache
    serves every ship and every later search; the craft-dependent floor (escape, capture) stays a cheap closed form over
    the cell's excesses;
  - where the cache lives (T228's STM cache, or one per catalogue);
  - eviction (clear at the game's GC point);
  - the lattice moving the valleys' sampled cells, so windows found can shift by a cell (the tests' numbers move).
- Measure the scan's share of planning time first (LR012).

entries.title: Exact memo of the burn integrators: a cache in an STM monad, threaded through the planner
entries.body:
The second of A183's two steps. One map per burn integrator in `stm-containers` (1.2.2 in the pinned nixpkgs): keyed by a
product type of the inputs' exact bits (`castDoubleToWord64`, so that −0 and NaN keep the exact semantics), `Hashable`,
values stored lazily.
- **Threading.** The cache is created once and threaded through the planner in an STM monad (Reader over STM or IO; no
  `unsafePerformIO`). Event forms, constraints, gate readings, the residual handed to Newton, and strategies' offers all
  become monadic, and the lazy per-reading memo in `Values` becomes explicit.
- **Eviction.** Clear the cache, with a manual GC point the game calls after planning.
- **Keys.** Build the key outside any atomic update: building one can run further integrations.
- **Memory.** About 10,000 distinct burns per planning run with boxed samples; after T215, measure peak memory.

*2026-10-02, phase 1 done another way (merge 1011b4d):* no cache. A Jacobian column also shares an event whose declared
inputs read the same as the base's: the moved variable is not among them, the events it reads are shared, and the ledger
carries the same craft. The spiral capture on a falling entry declares its reads. Electric mission solve 2.03 s (3.49 s
after T227, 3.83 s before), member identical; six scenarios byte-identical. Left for phase 2, the STM cache: span
columns (the mass really changes), the fall settled twice in one reading (entry and fall), line-search trials, and
refinement's repeats across strategies and probes.

*2026-10-02, profiled (T231):* refinement is about 90% of a run, half of it contract probing; the full solve and the flown
menu are about 11%. Phase 2 should aim at refinement's probes, after T231's explicit sharing.

*2026-10-03:* The memo was for repeated flights during planning, which R001 moves out of planning. Revisit if repeated integrations show in the full solve's profile.

entries.title: Pure Jacobian reuse: a finite-difference column's reading shares the base reading's results for events its variable cannot reach
entries.body:
Merge ec39f3b.
- **Declaring.** Events declare `reads` (variables, events, and other events' ledger), `Unknown` by default and never
  shared.
- **The plan.** `Skeleton.sharingPlan` holds each event's dependency closure: its variables, plus what it reads, plus every
  burn and shed before it and before each ledger point it reads.
- **Reading.** `readWith` gives a declared event a restricted reading, so an undeclared read returns nothing. Given a base
  reading and the perturbed variable, it shares the base's memo and ledger entry, as one, for every event whose closure
  misses that variable.
- **Solving.** `Newton.Problem` has `columns`; `Full` reads the Jacobian's columns and the seed's probes through it.

Declared: the order, the spiral escape, the low-thrust cruise (whose coast is now read only where the blocks meet) and a
falling entry. Six scenarios and 208 tests byte-identical; electric mission solve 3.49 s (3.83 s), member identical.

Findings:
- The closure table must be a lazy map: built strict, it forced closures that refer to each other, and the low-ceiling
  scenario looped.
- Most of the electric solve's remaining cost is the fall's two re-settles, downstream of every cruise variable: T228's
  case.
- Other legs: T229.

entries.title: Declare the remaining legs' reads so their Jacobian columns share (T227's follow-up)
entries.body:
- **A coarse declaration.** `Reads` gains `Prior`: the named variables, and any event listed before with its ledger,
  resolved over the skeleton in `sharingPlan`. `Refine.declaredLeg` gives every leg's undeclared events `Prior` over the
  leg's own variables.
- **The one cross-leg read.** The asymptotic entry reads the capture's `rp` and `plane` after it, and names them. With
  the entry declared, byte-identity found no other.

Six scenarios and 208 tests byte-identical.

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Torch | 1.00 s | 0.96 s |
| Helium-3 torch parked high | 5.86 s | 5.48 s |
| Low-ceiling torch | 10.82 s | 10.58 s |
| Test suite | 27.5 s | 22.9 s |

The scenarios gain little: their full solves are a small share of a run beside refinement, the probes and the cheap tier.
Measure where the time goes before T228 phase 2.

entries.title: Step 2b: the arrival hyperbola
entries.body:
The closed forms a capture is read from, in canonical units and generic for `ad`: the hyperbola from its excess and
aim, the state at a radius, the fall time, the capture kick. Tested against the kernel. Split from the capture leg
(2c) on 2026-10-05. Design note: `docs/plans/rebuild/step-2b-hyperbola.md`, reviewed by Shaun 2026-10-05 (formulas brought across; seed-centred angles; the aim's axis the further of the pole and an equatorial axis).

`Iapetus.Hyperbola` and its twelve tests (40 new-code tests, the whole suite 248). Built in vectors from the asymptote;
`stateAt` takes 1 − cos ν directly, since √(1 − cos²) lost half the digits at periapsis (caught by the periapsis law).
The kernel's capture burn and fall time are brought across and serve as oracles through the unit boundary; the fall time
is also checked by the kernel's Kepler propagation reaching periapsis, and the kick by the energy after it. A
deliberate fault in p̂ fails the asymptote law.

entries.title: B-plane reference axes, and directions as variables

meta.consult-when: choosing the B-plane's reference axis or an aim's zero, an arrival or departure near a body's pole, a direction (asymptote, thrust aim) as solve variables, or a solve that moves far from its seed

entries.body:
A short literature check (2026-10-05) behind step 2b's "Angles and axes", with the sources listed there: JPL's 2019
B-plane poster (Bradley), AGI's and STK's B-plane documentation, FreeFlyer's guide, a tangent-plane retraction for
unit vectors (arXiv 2504.08252), and Ceres's and GTSAM's manifold parameterisations.

**Takeaways:**
- **The B-plane is conventionally aligned with the body's pole,** and tools let a caller give another reference
  frame instead. It is singular where the asymptote lies along the reference axis.
- **The B-plane is known to be used inconsistently;** JPL developed alternative frames for its navigation software
  (2019). The poster gives no detail of them.
- **A unit vector as a variable:** two numbers in the tangent plane, mapped back by a retraction. Ceres and GTSAM
  re-centre that chart at every step. A chart fixed at the seed keeps variables' meaning fixed through a solve, which
  holds and R002 need; re-centring is the next step if a solve must move far.
- **For any body:** angles in a frame centred on the seed, and the aim's axis whichever of the pole and an equatorial
  axis lies further from the seed asymptote (never within 45°, no tuned threshold).

entries.title: Several menu entries in one trace, switchable in the viewer
entries.body:
- Trace v2 gains an optional top-level `flights` array, backward
  compatibly: each element carries what a single document carries per
  flight (`title`, the route's menu `labels`, `tags`, `measures` in SI,
  `summary`, `path`), the first flight stays at the top level exactly as
  before, and `catalog` and `rendering` stay once. `Trace.Document` holds
  a `Flight` record and `documentValue`/`writeFlights` over a non-empty
  list; `traceValue` for one flight renders byte for byte what it did, and
  the array is written only for two or more flights, so the committed
  Earth-to-Mars trace regenerates unchanged. Documented in
  `docs/archive/catalog-loading.md`.
- `iapetus-trace --export shown|front|all` solves from the seeds, lowers
  and flies every entry of the set through the same pipeline as the pick,
  writes them into one document with the pick first, prints one
  lowering/flight block per entry in menu order and how many were written;
  an entry whose full solve cannot start or whose lowering fails is
  reported and left out. The torch's shown set (the cheap window and the
  direct brachistochrone) exports in 12 s; the nuclear-thermal stage's
  whole priced menu, four routes, in 9 s.
- The viewer shows a flight selector in the panel when a document carries
  several flights, labelled by the tags and the menu's measures
  ("cheapest · 617.0 d · 6.9 t"). Switching makes the chosen flight the
  trace (`Trace.selectFlight`), rebuilds the drawn path on a fresh scene,
  the flight list and the validator verdict, re-runs the conformance and
  energy checks, and resets the clock to the flight's start, the focus to
  its first arc's body, play stopped and the camera where the page opens.
  `scene.js` is untouched. `window.iapetus.trace` is the current flight;
  `window.iapetus.flights` gives the count and index.
- Tests: the byte identity and a two-flight round trip through
  `Trace.Json` in `test/Main.hs` (209 pass); a Playwright spec,
  `test/web-browser/flights.spec.js`, over a document served from
  `IAPETUS_FLIGHTS_URL` that checks the selector lists two, that switching
  changes the arc count and resets the clock, focus and camera, and that
  the conformance check passes for both; the existing trace spec passes
  against the two-flight document too.

entries.title: Viewer camera: the rest of the survey
entries.body:
From `docs/archive/viewer-camera-notes.md`: double-click a body to focus it, zoom to the cursor,

entries.title: The viewer's camera as a turntable with north up
entries.body:
- The viewer's `OrbitControls` orbited about the camera's default `+y`,
  a direction in the ecliptic, and let the elevation reach within a
  microradian of its pole, where a fixed-up camera's horizontal basis
  collapses and a pixel of drag spins the view. Replaced by a hand-written
  `Turntable` in `static/scene.js`: azimuth about the catalogue's `+z`,
  elevation clamped to ±89°, log-distance; the focus is always the scene's
  origin, so there is no pan. Drag is a constant 0.005 rad/px, the wheel
  dollies by ×1.25 per notch toward the focus, one finger orbits and two
  pinch through pointer events. Every change of goal is eased with one
  0.12 s time constant, which gives the drag its inertia and makes a change
  of focus a smooth zoom that keeps the view's direction.
- The survey behind the choice — Blender's turntable and trackball, Three's
  Orbit, Trackball and Arcball controls, Celestia, Universe Sandbox,
  SpaceEngine and KSP — is `docs/archive/viewer-camera-notes.md`.
- `test/web-browser/camera.spec.js`: a drag far past either pole stops at
  the clamp with a finite quaternion, a level horizon and the same
  radians-per-pixel azimuth response; the wheel shortens the distance
  monotonically by the notch factor down to the floor without turning;
  changing focus to the root, the last frame and the ship keeps azimuth,
  elevation and direction.

entries.title: The viewer's camera is a turntable with north up

meta.revisit-if: the viewer needs pan, or a free-flying camera

entries.body:
**Question** _(None asked: settled while building T081.)_ The viewer's `OrbitControls`
orbited about a direction in the ecliptic and let the elevation reach within a
microradian of its pole, where a pixel of drag spins the view.

**Answer** A hand-written `Turntable` in `static/scene.js`: azimuth about the
catalogue's `+z`, elevation clamped to ±89°, log-distance, the focus always the scene's
origin (no pan), drag at 0.005 rad/px, the wheel dollying ×1.25 per notch, every change
of goal eased with one 0.12 s time constant.

**Why** A fixed-up camera's horizontal basis collapses at the pole; a turntable with a
clamp never reaches it, and keeps the system's north up.

**Alternatives considered** From the survey in `docs/archive/viewer-camera-notes.md`: Blender's
turntable and trackball, Three's Orbit, Trackball and Arcball controls, Celestia,
Universe Sandbox, SpaceEngine and KSP.
